Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

📅 2026-08-25 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch. It runs over your real code, lets your team edit anything visually, and puts agents to work on content, accessibility, and the maintenance you never get to. Incubated at Strapi. Thank you!

Recent findings suggest that every website is at its best the day it ships. The final branch merges, the site goes live exactly as designed, and it is briefly perfect. It will never be this good again.

According to recent reports, not because anything breaks. The site keeps working. But the market moves, the messaging shifts, a competitor launches something, and the careful thing you built slowly stops matching the company it represents. A year later, it is a period piece. Not broken, just behind. Every team knows this decay, and almost everyone treats it as a law of nature.

Sources indicate that it doesn’t have to be that way. A website could keep improving after launch instead of drifting away from its best day, quietly optimizing itself while the team that built it works on something else.

Picture it working: while you sleep, an agent catches that last week’s design-system change never propagated to the pricing page, and fixes it. Another finds a set of images shipped uncompressed in a rushed release and optimizes them. A third flags an accessibility regression a newly introduced component introduced, and either fixes it or leaves it for you to check. You wake up to a site that is measurably better than the one you left, and a short list of the few decisions the agents wanted your eyes on. That is the version worth wanting.

And the moment you take that promise seriously, you run into a problem that has nothing to do with the technology:.

It has been revealed that the obvious move, once you have capable agents, is to hand them the whole site. Let them write, edit, optimize, and publish, and get out of the way. It sounds like the natural endpoint, and it is the first thing most people picture when they hear “autonomous website.”.

It is also the thing almost nobody wants once it is real in front of them.

We learned this the way you learn most things worth knowing: by building the opposite first. Building Fimo, an autonomous website platform, we set out to make websites fully autonomous, assumed that was the goal, and then watched what people actually did with it. What they did was hesitate. Not because they distrusted the agents, but because a website has no single owner. Different parts belong to different people, and each one wants a different amount of autonomy. So the question was never whether to trust the agents. It was where to draw the line, and for whom.

Once you ask it that way, the work splits cleanly into three kinds.

Recent findings suggest that start with the largest pile, because it is bigger than people expect. Most of what keeps a website healthy is rule-bound, repetitive, and completely joyless. Keeping accessibility compliant as pages change. Propagating a design-system patch once a token moves. Catching a broken meta tag, an unoptimized image, a link that rotted when a URL changed three sprints ago.

In a recent development, none of this is where anyone’s talent lives. Nobody was hired because of their gift for spotting a missing alt attribute. This is the work you are actively relieved to hand off, and it is the work agents are best at, because it is defined by rules rather than taste. An agent that quietly keeps this layer correct across a whole site, unattended, is not a threat to anyone’s job. It is the tedious eighty percent finally taken care of.

Naming how much of the maintenance load actually lives in this pile is what makes the whole idea of an autonomous site feel less like a leap. You are not handing over judgment. You are handing over chores.

At the other end sits the work you would not delegate at any price. It is a small pile, but it is the reason you exist.

Industry observers note that an agent can check a fresh page against every rule you have given it. It can confirm the contrast passes, the heading order is right, the tokens are correct, the copy matches the style guide. What it cannot do is decide what the page should feel like, or whether the thing you are shipping is, in the taste sense, good. That judgment is exactly what you were hired for, and no amount of capability moves it off your desk.

In a recent development, this is the part people reach for first when they resist autonomy, and they are right to protect it. The mistake is thinking the whole site is made of this kind of work. Almost none of it is. But that small part matters more than all the rest, which is why automating everything feels so wrong.

Between the chores and the untouchable sits the part no product can settle for you, because the line runs through different places for different people.

Notice what is happening there. It isn’t that one of them is cautious and the other reckless. It is that the same task carries different amounts of judgment for each of them. For one person it is a decision; for the other it is a chore. There is no default a product could ship that would be right for both, because “right” is a function of where your value sits, not of the task itself.

Industry observers note that this is why the control has to be per-task and per-person, and why we stopped trying to find the setting that would work for everyone. There isn’t one. There is only the line each person draws, and the tools to draw it precisely.

Sources indicate that once you accept that the line is personal, a toggle between “approve” and “delegate” stops being enough. Where the line sits depends on what the agent is actually doing, so the real unit of control is the agent itself.

This is where it stopped being a settings problem, and it is the shape Fimo took. You don’t pick from a fixed menu of behaviors. You compose the agents, deciding what each one is even allowed to touch. You can build one from scratch, or take one close to your needs and shape it to your own line: an accessibility agent you trust to run unattended, a content agent you keep close to anything brand-facing.

And they don’t stay fixed. They learn from their tasks and from what you teach them, so the boundary you set last month isn’t the one you’re stuck with. What you had to approve then, you can delegate now, not because you lowered your guard but because the agent earned it. The line is not a setting you configure once. It moves as trust is earned, in the direction of less work for you.

Sources indicate that none of this means flipping a site to autonomous on day one. In practice it goes the other way. You delegate a little, watch how it does, and loosen.

And you can actually watch. Every agent’s runs, its history, its logs, and a before-and-after of what it changed are there to inspect. Trust doesn’t grow because you got used to the idea; it grows because you can see what happened and compare. The first time an agent quietly fixes something you would have missed, and you can see exactly what it did, the next delegation gets easier.

Deadlines keep you from becoming the bottleneck on what you have already handed over. If you don’t weigh in, the agent proceeds. You set the terms once, and you stop being the thing the whole site waits on.

The worry people voice first is that an agent will change something on their site without them. Turn it around: the real risk is a site that never changes at all. A frozen site doesn’t stay safe. It just falls behind, slowly, in a way nobody notices until it represents a manufacturer that no longer exists.

It has been revealed that the point of autonomy was never to remove you from your website. It was to remove the decay.

Industry observers note that the point of autonomy is to keep the launch-day version from being the best version, and to let you spend your judgment on the handful of things that actually deserve it, while the rest takes care of itself. Draw the line where your value is. Let the agents hold everything on the other side of it. And let the line move as they prove they can.

Breaking: Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences.
  • Sources indicate that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

Sources indicate that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

Industry observers note that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Fresh York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the Upcoming Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

In a recent development, for today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her upcoming installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

In a recent development, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

“The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

It has been revealed that the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she says. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

Industry observers note that that initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

In a recent development, what began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas says. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas states. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Fresh York.

In a recent development, neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

According to recent reports, A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

In a recent development, phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

According to recent reports, A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

#34321. ‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (848 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali has formed a one-woman band.
  • Industry observers note that it was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art.
  • Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali has formed a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

Industry observers note that it was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative.

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she states. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Industry observers note that rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali claims. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”.

In a recent development, informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”.

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

According to recent reports, shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?

My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

Sources indicate that the culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

#34320. Latest Update: Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2983 w)

Latest Update: Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that in organisations today, data has never been more available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently. Her background in … More about Meriem ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that in organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction.

When that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all.

Data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional.

For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you.

Recent findings suggest that in 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different.

Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal.

But visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative. The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about?

It has been revealed that one of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics. Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline.

Before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss.

Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio: every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal.

In a recent development, for a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context, under specific pressure. Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is.

Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it.

Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart.

That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on.

The high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project.

Most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible.

According to recent reports, defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric, a population, and an implied action. That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely.

In a recent development, starting with available data produces a dashboard that answers no particular question, because it was never built for one — every number is present, none of them pointed anywhere. Starting with the operational question does the reverse: every element on the screen earns its place, because each one is there to help answer it.

For example, consider a UX team trying to fix a leaky checkout flow for an e-commerce website. A data-first approach pulls everything available, from clicks to scroll depth and device types, yielding a massive dashboard that leaves everyone asking, “Okay, but what do we actually change?” A context-first approach starts with a constraint: “At which step of the checkout do users drop off?” By filtering out 90% of the noise, the team builds a simple funnel chart, instantly spots a bottleneck on the payment screen, and knows exactly what to redesign.

Designing for an audience comes down to two things: accountability and familiarity.

According to recent reports, familiarity is about data literacy. Do they read charts instinctively, or does a complex visualisation create friction? Handing a dense, multi-layered dashboard to a Head of Sales and a senior analyst is like giving the same map to someone who navigates by landmarks and someone who reads grid coordinates. The data is accurate, but it is only functional for one of them.

Accountability dictates how that complexity must be presented. A chart showing a 12% decline carries vastly different weight for the executive responsible for that number versus the analyst simply reporting it. Understanding your audience means grasping this relationship; data is never processed neutrally when your performance is on the line.

Together, familiarity and accountability decide one practical thing: how much you can put in front of someone.

In data visualisation, simplicity is not a fixed virtue — the right level of it is contingent on who is reading, and what they need to do.

An analyst relies on a high-density environment to conduct diagnostic discovery. By isolating individual behaviour nodes and mapping out raw user flows, they interrogate the data at its atomic level to uncover the hidden insights and underperforming spend that will shape future campaigns.

Recent findings suggest that an executive, by contrast, requires a highly synthesised translation of that data to immediately identify what is driving commercial growth. Tailoring a dashboard to your audience means adjusting the density dial, delivering maximum signal with appropriate complexity for the specific brain in the room.

Sources indicate that most data projects operate on the comfortable assumption that if a chart is accurate and clear, the insight will take care of itself. In reality, information and insight are entirely different states. Information is what the data demonstrates, whereas insight is the specific decision, shift in understanding, or course correction someone makes as a result of seeing it. If the intended business change isn’t defined before the design begins, a dashboard will default to passive reporting rather than driving action.

Marketing and engineering teams experience the danger of this gap whenever a core business metric suddenly plummets.

A dashboard built for information simply sounds the alarm, showing a chart that tracks a sharp 15% drop in booking rates. Because the data lacks depth, leadership defaults to panic: they immediately call the UX design team, assuming the app is broken or the checkout flow is flawed. Because the data doesn’t pinpoint the core of the problem, it triggers a costly, misplaced fire drill.

Sources indicate that A dashboard built for insight isolates the variables required to make an informed decision. Instead of a single, flat booking metric, the visualisation maps the drop against traffic sources and campaign rolls out — instantly revealing that while app performance and core user conversion are perfectly stable, the sitewide rate was artificially diluted by a massive influx of low-intent click traffic from a newly scaled campaign. The team doesn’t waste time redesigning a functioning app; they get the exact insight needed to pause the underperforming marketing campaign and adjust their acquisition strategy.

Every visualisation implies a next step, even if that step is “nothing needs to change right now.” The question is whether the design makes that implication clear enough for the viewer to recognise it.

My aha moment in data visualisation happened during a project for a client-facing B2B SaaS platform focused on enterprise talent management and competency tracking in Pegasystems skills. The platform captured a massive footprint of daily telemetry, and the brief arrived open-ended: “We have an immense archive of user activity, now we need to present it to enterprise teams.”.

According to recent reports, we could very easily have charted everything that was captured, but we wouldn’t be doing end people any favours if they just ended up looking at a data graveyard. My responsibility immediately moved beyond pure interface craftsmanship; it became about architecting a highly practical tool for real people who would open this dashboard routinely and need it to tell them an honest, immediate story about their workflows.

Here is how the project actually went.

The client believed this massive pool of data could help their customers perform better, and wanted an interface that finally enabled that growth. Translating that broad ambition into tangible visualisations required defining the practical mechanics of performance. What variables indicate advancement vs passive usage? What does “perform better” actually mean? How do you measure it?

In a recent development, an obvious candidate was time spent by product. Every platform tracks it. It is easy to show, and it feels meaningful. But time spent is a proxy; it tells you someone was there, not whether they got anything out of it.

The more meaningful signals were competency scores by area, certification completion rates, and historical performance trajectories. Integrating time-spent data alongside these performance metrics added a useful layer of interpretation, helping us surface which modules people were underutilising and whether that directly correlated with lagging scores. Time spent became a supporting signal in the larger story.

Industry observers note that the second question was about the appropriate level of granularity. An identical metric carries completely different weight depending on who is looking at it. An individual contributor tracking their own completion rate needs to know if they are pacing correctly, whereas a manager reviewing a team aggregate needs to know precisely who requires immediate support. This distinction shaped every subsequent data-exposure and filtering decision. Defining that structural story early determined exactly what to show, and to whom.

Recent findings suggest that the most straightforward approach to this design would have been predictable: use the same charts, but offer an individual view and an aggregated team view. Far too many dashboards rely on this shortcut, subtly tweaking the scale of identical data visualisations and labelling it “personalisation.”.

According to recent reports, an authentic analysis of the audience reveals a much deeper rift. Frontline team leads and individual contributors required distinct narrative structures and design principles.

Recent findings suggest that having used e-learning platforms myself, I remember the frustration of opening a tool without a clear sense of my current standing, core strengths, or slipping metrics. That personal experience directly guided the individual contributor workspace; it needed to act as a highly tailored, self-directed mirror that was granular, honest, and personal.

Industry observers note that conversely, the manager’s interface had to bypass individual milestones initially to provide a macro pulse check on team vulnerabilities. It was designed around a different operational reality: how is the group progressing, and where are the consistent gaps? The view prioritised the aggregate picture first, while retaining an intuitive path to drill down into tactical day-to-day coordination when needed.

Our insight strategy was locked in during the early conceptual phase, long before wireframing a single chart. We intentionally abandoned the idea of building a dense, passive data log and focused on pacing the narrative arc.

For individual contributors, the core value was self-direction, ensuring they could glance at the interface on a Monday morning and immediately derive a clear priority list for the week ahead.

For managers, the goal was to fundamentally shift the timing of operational conversations, providing them with the necessary baseline to intervene before a skill gap evolved into a critical project failure. The visualisations needed to surface the exact moments when a human check-in would be useful, shifting their workflow from reactive post-mortems to proactive guidance.

According to recent reports, the comparison tool was the highlight nobody had asked for. A manager dashboard and an individual dashboard are easy to anticipate. What is harder to land is: what if a manager wants to compare two specific team members against the same metrics, side by side? That view came from a design assumption, and it turned out to be the feature that resonated most.

The decisions that mattered most in this project weren’t in the initial brief — capturing data they hadn’t thought to request, and structuring it to answer questions they had not previously known how to articulate, which is the core differentiator of a user-centric data strategy.

According to recent reports, the choice of visualisation layout must follow the geometric nature of the data itself. For this project, the core design problem was enabling an individual user to answer a specific question at a single glance: across eight distinct competency areas, where are my relative strengths and gaps?

It has been revealed that to solve this, we mapped the data using a radar chart. By organising multiple variables across axes radiating from a central point using polar coordinates, the interface connects the data points to form a single, unified shape. An even, balanced polygon instantly signals well-rounded proficiency, while a sharply skewed shape draws the eye immediately to an outlier area.

While a traditional linear bar chart would have forced the viewer to scan eight individual bars and mentally calculate the variance, a concentric, radial layout segments the data layers to make progress tracking and skill gaps immediately readable. When all dimensions share an identical scale and scoring method, the radar chart is not an unconventional aesthetic choice — it is the most functional tool for multi-dimensional analysis.

The colour system was the other decision made early, and I mean early. During the branding exercise, each of the three products was assigned a colour. That colour did not stay in the brand guidelines. It was built into the data model from the beginning, running consistently across every chart, every filter, every breakdown. By the time a user landed on the dashboard for the first time, the mental model was already in place. They had not been taught the language. They already knew it.

The shift from passive information to active insight demonstrated up first in how the dashboard was actually used. Following the deployment of the personalised dashboards and side-by-side team comparison tools, weekly active engagement on the platform’s analytics features rose noticeably, per internally reported figures. Managers were no longer opening the tool once a month to pull static reports. They were using it every Monday morning to actively plan their week.

In a recent development, revenue and user growth also moved in the right direction over the following two quarters, though — as with most single-project outcomes — it’s hard to isolate the dashboard’s exact contribution from everything else that changed at the same time. The client reported churn across the platform falling to one of its lowest points on record. The clearest evidence of impact came from qualitative feedback. Managers reported that instead of using data to dissect a ‘bad’ month after the fact, the visualisations allowed them to instantly spot slipping performance and schedule a quick supportive catch-up before it turned into a real gap.

It has been revealed that data design reaches its full potential when visual presentation is treated as an upstream architectural choice rather than a downstream formatting step. Bringing structured UX thinking to data turns visualisations into active decision-making engines, ensuring every chart, report, and metric directly serves a human purpose:.

Recent findings suggest that the next time you are tasked with creating a data visualisation — whether it is an enterprise dashboard, an executive report, or a public-facing infographic — step away from the design canvas and BI tools. Focus your initial effort on the human decisions behind the screen. Only then will your data stop being a passive log of the past and start driving the direction of the future.

Industry News: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when we introduced The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • In a recent development, as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • In a recent development, what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when we introduced The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

In a recent development, as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

In a recent development, what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

We spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

According to recent reports, in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

In a recent development, confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a major believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

According to recent reports, clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to initiative? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

This sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

Industry observers note that my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

My conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

Sources indicate that we talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Industry observers note that listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

Sources indicate that in my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

Sources indicate that if you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, fresh perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Industry observers note that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Substantial Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a upcoming group exhibition.

It has been revealed that an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

According to recent reports, titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Industry observers note that the results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

In a recent development, candelabra by Fort Standard, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

Participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Company, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Candelabra by Hanna Anonen, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Click through the gallery above for a closer look at works featured in the exhibition.

According to recent reports, the exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Industry observers note that timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

It has been revealed that candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, Latest York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

Candelabra by Dustin Barzell, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.
  • The gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL.
  • In a recent development, the answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

The gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

In a recent development, the answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

The system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

Recent findings suggest that the caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Sources indicate that of course, presentation matters, too.
  • Recent findings suggest that italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Sources indicate that of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Recent findings suggest that italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Sources indicate that perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

It has been revealed that from Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

In a recent development, from cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Sources indicate that porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

Recent findings suggest that long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

Sources indicate that still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of Maison Plage.

Industry observers note that for 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Rizzoli.

For a century, The Fresh Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The Latest Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

Photography courtesy of Thames & Hudson.

Food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of teNeues.

Not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Recent findings suggest that from Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.

Recent findings suggest that LIFE. Let’s Dance is available at taschen.com for $50.

Photography courtesy of Wynwood Walls.

From the streets of Paris to collaborations with Chanel and Louis Vuitton, André Saraiva has built a career around his playful, instantly recognizable graffiti character, Mr. A. Published by Rizzoli, Graffiti Life explores the artist’s creative world through painting, photography, graphic design, fashion, and more. The 320-page hardcover is as expressive as its subject, featuring a vibrant cloth cover with foil lettering and seven pop-ups designed by Saraiva himself. It’s a colorful, interactive celebration of an artist who has never been one to stay within the lines.

André Saraiva: Graffiti Life is available at shop.thewynwoodwalls.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Printworks.

The most meaningful coffee table book might be the one you fill yourself. Designed to look like a traditional art book, Printworks’ Life Photo Book features a minimalist beige cloth cover with understated white typography. Inside, 40 sheets of high-quality photo paper offer space to preserve favorite memories, from everyday moments to once-in-a-lifetime adventures. Its expandable binding accommodates photographs as they’re added, transforming a beautifully designed object into a personal keepsake.

The Life Photo Book is available at printworksmarket.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

It has been revealed that what does contemporary product design look like around the world? Phaidon’s Designed for Life offers a fascinating look at 100 designers pushing the boundaries of furniture, lighting, everyday objects, and more. From established names like Faye Toogood and Sabine Marcelis to emerging talents, the 304-page hardcover explores the materials, techniques, and ideas shaping design today. With 500 illustrations, it’s an inspiring addition to any design enthusiast’s coffee table.

Designed for Life: The World’s Best Product Designers is available at store.hermanmiller.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Recent findings suggest that japanese architect Sou Fujimoto has spent his career challenging the boundaries between architecture and nature, creating structures that blur the lines between indoors and out. Published by Taschen, Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today explores three decades of his experimental approach through projects including London’s Serpentine Gallery Pavilion, L’Arbre Blanc in Montpellier, and the Grand Ring at Expo 2025 Osaka. Filled with architectural photography, drawings, and sketches, the oversized, 464-page volume documents the evolution of one of contemporary architecture’s most inventive minds.

It has been revealed that fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today is available for preorder at taschen.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Sources indicate that few people have shaped fashion imagery quite like Grace Coddington. In Grace: The American Vogue Years, the legendary creative director revisits some of her most memorable editorials from 2002 to 2016, including collaborations with photographers Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, and Tim Walker. More than 350 photographs showcase Coddington’s imaginative approach to fashion storytelling, while her behind-the-scenes commentary reveals how the elaborate shoots came together. This updated edition offers a fascinating look at the creative vision behind some of Vogue’s most iconic images.

Grace: The American Vogue Years is available at phaidon.com for $60.

Photography courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Industry observers note that from maximalist spaces bursting with color to minimalist interiors that celebrate simplicity, Defining Style explores the many ways we make a space our own. Written by Joan Barzilay Freund, the book examines 25 distinct design styles through 150 residential interiors by designers, including spaces by Studio Shamshiri, Laura Gonzalez, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, as well as artist Móyòsóré Martins’ studio. With 260 illustrations and a vibrant, geometric cover, it’s as visually engaging on the coffee table as the spaces featured inside.

Defining Style: The Book of Interior Design is available at phaidon.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Art history gets a playful makeover in Assouline’s Art Game Book, which brings an interactive twist to the traditional coffee table book. Through quizzes, puzzles, games, and essays, author David Rosenberg takes readers from Cubism and Dada to Pop Art and contemporary digital art, featuring icons like Warhol, Basquiat, and Dalí along the way. Newly updated for 2026, the oversized, canvas-bound hardcover makes learning about art feel more like play than homework.

The Art Game Book is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Industry observers note that color takes center stage in Rainbow Dreams, a vibrant exploration of how contemporary artists use the full spectrum to transform their work. Featuring more than 200 artworks by over 100 artists, including Yayoi Kusama, Takashi Murakami, Olafur Eliasson, and Ugo Rondinone, the book spans painting, sculpture, photography, and immersive installations. The 256-page hardcover is a colorful design object in its own right, with a seamless rainbow gradient wrapping around the cover and edges. It’s a joyful addition to any art lover’s collection.

Rainbow Dreams: Color and Light in Contemporary Art is available at phaidon.com for $40.
