📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the best 3D scanners have changed the game for custom manufacturing, and they continue to advance. Creality, which also makes some of the best 3D printers, already has a wide range of solutions, including the versatile Sermoon P1S.

Industry observers note that now, it's added to the family a new device that looks set up to speed up workflows for those working in automobile custromisation. The Raptor Pro Max builds on the existing Raptor Pro handheld scanner but almost doubles the number of cross blue laser lines and unlocks a 40% larger single capture range.

The Raptor Pro Max has 42 cross blue laser lines, up from 22 on the Raptor Pro, and it can reach up to 1.26 million measurements, raising the maximum scanning rate by approximately 91% while offering a single capture range of up to 480 × 330 mm at a working distance of 550 mm.

In a recent development, that wider coverage and higher scanning rate mean that you can capture more of a bumper, door or body panel in each pass, which gives successive frames more shared geometry to maintain stable tracking. The expanded coverage also helps reduce the number of markers required by up to 25%.

Recent findings suggest that creality states the reduction of repeat passes, the need for repositioning and the application of markers means users can complete scans of automotive workpieces in up to 40% less time. That will allow custom parts to be moved into design and trial-fitting work more quickly.

Sources indicate that for smaller features, there's also the option to switch to seven parallel blue laser lines to capture edges, threads, and chamfers. Together, the two blue laser modes cover objects from 5 to 4,000 mm in size. Creality cites volumetric accuracy of 0.02 mm + 0.08 mm/m.² The blue lasers can also capture suitable black and metallic surfaces without scanning spray.

Recent findings suggest that during handheld scanning, real-time preview in Creality Scan lets operators monitor coverage as they move around a part. The Blue Laser Line Mode operates at up to 60 fps and the a near-infrared (NIR) structured-light mode at up to 30 fps, with geometry or texture tracking. There's built-in anti-shake functionality to help reduce the impact of hand movement.

Industry observers note that the Creality Raptor Pro Max has a suggested retail price of $1,799, which is reduced by around 10% for a limited time to $1,619. There's also a limited-time bundle including a Scan Bridge for $1,799.

Check out the Creality US store or UK store for more details.

There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

#34300. Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📅 2026-10-20 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

Industry observers note that as someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a big part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is presently rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

According to recent reports, and my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Recent findings suggest that because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

Take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

To see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

The random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

Industry observers note that the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

Normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

In the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

According to recent reports, there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

According to recent reports, this can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

When I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

Think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

One quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader users get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

In a recent development, I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

In a recent development, if you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

We’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

Recent findings suggest that for dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Sources indicate that here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

Industry observers note that some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

But! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

Recent findings suggest that if someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Industry observers note that whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

Tech Report: Accordion Icons: Which Work Best?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Well, research highlights that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, users expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

It has been revealed that the rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a new page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

It’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow consumers to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

For accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

Recent findings suggest that the safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

But we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — highlights all options and allows users to drill down.

And if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.
  • The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces.
  • Sources indicate that grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Sources indicate that grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

It has been revealed that for Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

Industry observers note that the Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and at the moment serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely newly introduced collection,” Grynsztejn states, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

According to recent reports, during her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.

Tech Report: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

📅 2026-11-03 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch.

This was what it looked like before you made the change:.

See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off.

See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

None of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

In my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

It has been revealed that I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

Think of a upcoming CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only shows the first one:.

In a recent development, I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

Sources indicate that the essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

Recent findings suggest that I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That stated, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

The first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

Lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

And when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

Back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float problems. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our newly introduced tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

According to recent reports, according to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a fresh block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

That means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

The card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

In a recent development, this is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

Sources indicate that in the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

It has been revealed that in isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Before you add container-type to an element, ask yourself the following three questions:.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

The third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a new tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

The :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

According to recent reports, say we want to remove paragraph margins from card components that have a hero image. This might look like it does the job:.

See the Pen [Scenario 3: The Selector That Reached Too Far [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/pvexpRd) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It has been revealed that this card has no hero image. Yet every paragraph in it loses its margin.

If you inspect the comment’s paragraph in DevTools and look at the “Styles” pane, you will find two culprits:.

It could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that notes “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators:.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

Native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity claims the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

Plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

Industry observers note that don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your upcoming component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !vital keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

In a recent development, miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

None of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

Sources indicate that not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding issue, not a technology issue.”.

Sources indicate that I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

In a recent development, “We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe said it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

Moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

Take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group concern about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

Recent findings suggest that I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout patch each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

Sources indicate that first, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

Second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

Let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule indicates so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an concern, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

That is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

The same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

In a recent development, to be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

Sources indicate that each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

In a recent development, A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

None of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the new CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

Industry observers note that and the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

It has been revealed that this gap between a clean start and a real codebase demonstrates up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge concern,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

In a recent development, most of what we read about a latest feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

Sources indicate that before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the new tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

According to recent reports, modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a new capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

So, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

The Specsavers GTA 6 campaign is hilariously on brand

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The optical chain Specsavers has turned out to be an unlikely exception.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, GTA VI trendjacking was already everywhere, even before today's release of the most- anticipated video game in history (see our GTA VI review for our Digital Art Editor's experience playing it). A lot of the attempts to jump on the bandwagon have been lazy and half-hearted, with brands merely using AI image generators to give product shots a vaporwave makeover.

The optical chain Specsavers has turned out to be an unlikely exception. Its unusual GTA VI campaign might actually be the best brand collaboration of the year.

A post shared by Specsavers (@specsavers).

Recent findings suggest that that's right, Specsavers has entered into its "biggest partnership of all time’. It's sponsoring GTA... just not that GTA.

In a recent development, the teaser post above might have raised eyebrows among gamers given that GTA VI developer and publisher Rockstar Games has very limited collaborations. There's it's deal with the Miami Heat (and with Oakley for the GTA VI Collector's Edition), but there are only parody fake brands in GTA VI itself.

But Specsavers isn't sponsoring the video game that everyone's talking about. It's hooked up with GTA Transport Ltd, a British road haulage company based in Leicester. Which sounds a bit like Leonida, right?

“It might not be the GTA partnership I originally had in mind but a deal’s a deal. I'm pleased to offer every driver at GTA Transport a free eye test,” the manufacturer's brand partnerships and sponsorships lead Neil Liddle said.

Bugz Singh from GTA Transport Ltd said: “We were surprised when Specsavers got in touch, but we’re delighted to be the GTA they’ve teamed up with. Our drivers spend all day on the road, so they’re looking forward to their eye tests.”.

A post shared by Specsavers (@specsavers).

According to recent reports, specsavers' stunt rises above most of the GTA VI trendjacking that we've seen. It's funny, and it's a lot more creative and memorable than simply throwing Vice City hues onto brand imagery. Best of all, it shows that Specsavers really knows its brand and its public, maintaining consistency with the message it's been using for over 20 years.

Industry observers note that specsavers has been telling the same joke since 2002, and it still works. In fact, it's become even more effective. The line 'Should've gone to Specsavers', coined by then in-house creative director Graham Daldry, is now so ingrained in the public consciousness that it no longer needs to be appended onto the campaign. It's already implied.

Having already sold close to 16 million copies before today's release, GTA VI is a cultural phenomenon with a reach that extends well beyond that of most games. An AI-generated vaporwave graphic can't make an unrelated brand a part of that, but Specsavers has shown that on-brand creative thinking can forge a memorable connection to the entertainment event of the year.

Industry News: Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
  • In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
  • “Nothing came of that,” states Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” states Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

In a recent development, but now, Brinkmann indicates his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

It has been revealed that “The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on latest findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”.

It has been revealed that the east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

According to recent reports, the rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”.

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail).

According to recent reports, vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main.

The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann states. “That was our basis.”.

It has been revealed that although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann says. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”.

In a recent development, they discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”.

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674).

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3.

None of these reliefs demonstrated the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

It has been revealed that the team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann indicates. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann indicates. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Sources indicate that brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

It is possible that the upcoming Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann states. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027.

Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

📅 2026-11-05 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you.

Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration.

It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here: It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more.

“Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, America.gov, Glean, and other similar websites and web apps:.

The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps. This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri.

Immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible.

There is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier.

I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs.

Industry observers note that built environments also extend to digital experiences, and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established:.

It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.

Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation.

Industry observers note that we live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations.

While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability.

It has been revealed that recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You:.

Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it:.

It has been revealed that visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know fresh content has appeared because:.

In a recent development, so, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions.

In a recent development, live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, glancing upwards to read the LLM response when it appears.

First, read this excellent article by TetraLogical if this is your first attempt at getting live region announcements working. They’re tricky to get right, and this article sets the record straight.

One common pitfall I want to call specific attention to is applying aria-live on each LLM response message. Don’t do this. Instead, use a dedicated live region area to announce each message’s content.

According to recent reports, the live region area should be placed at the end of the DOM and used for all live region messaging. This method is far more stable and reliable, which is important for ensuring everyone understands what the experience is communicating.

With that established: What we want to do is trigger a live region announcement when the LLM’s chat reply shows up in full on the screen.

This creates an outcome where you can read the message if you can see the screen, and hear or feel the message if you cannot.

There are a few things to do when creating a good user experience for the people who rely on these live region announcements. These considerations mean the difference between a compliant-yet-unusable outcome and something that genuinely works for the person using it.

Attempting to announce the message as it streams in may create a juddering and confusing experience that’s difficult for someone to parse.

It is better to wait until the message has completed streaming, and then announce the message’s content in full.

Recent findings suggest that responses from an LLM often take time to complete. Generally speaking, there are three ways to show a response is still processing:.

These experiences are typically only shown visually. If you cannot see the screen, it may lead to it feeling like the experience has stalled or crashed — especially if the response is for a large or complicated request that takes a while to work through.

To address this, we’ll want to use live region announcements:.

It has been revealed that if text is visually shown on the screen: Ensure a companion live region announcement is also triggered at the same time the loading message text is displayed. The text string for the live region announcement should be the same as what is shown visually, to be sure to ensure parity of experience:.

If a text-less loading animation is shown on the screen: Ensure the loading state is also communicated to assistive technology.

A live region announcement that mentions the reply is loading after a set amount of time will facilitate an equivalent experience for this interaction. It doesn’t have to be too verbose; the word “Loading” can suffice:.

Sources indicate that triggering the loading message five seconds after prompt submission seems to be the sweet spot, according to the inclusive user research I evaluated. You can then have your logic repeat the loading message every five seconds until the LLM completes its actual reply.

In a recent development, be sure to also announce the reply immediately as it finishes streaming. You don’t need to wait until the next five-second loading message cycle is complete.

Also consider randomly selecting from a set of different phrases that communicate that a response is being formulated after the initial “Loading” message is dispatched. This helps in scenarios where someone may think the loading experience itself has crashed or stalled.

Industry observers note that we’ll eventually be able to replace the technique TetraLogical outlined with ariaNotify(). It is a much-needed and welcome addition to the platform, and will drastically lower the hacks and headaches many developers encounter when creating and managing live region announcements.

According to recent reports, baseline lists the ariaNotify() method as having cross-browser availability at the time of this article’s publication. However, there are two factors to consider here:.

Also consider that while a polyfill for ariaNotify() is available, you need to factor in whether it has both:.

What this realistically means is holding off for a while on ariaNotify() in favor of the tried and true TetraLogical live region technique.

Headings are the most popular way people who use screen readers navigate around an experience. Because of this, I advocate for inserting visually-hidden headings before each chat message.

Here’s a simplified version of that in code:.

And here’s what the code might look like using the actual content from a human question and an LLM response:.

It has been revealed that so, why the “You said:”/”Cody said:” prefix? Remember the visual bias. Visually, we can see the left- or right-hand alignment of messages, used to indicate who is saying what.

The prefix serves the same purpose: identifying the message’s owner. This allows people to swiftly move through a conversation the same way someone might quickly scroll upwards to re-establish context, checking who mentioned what and when.

It has been revealed that using landmark regions to wrap the larger overall areas of your LLM chat experience helps people understand its overall layout. It can also enable quick screen reader navigation to each area:.

Sources indicate that landmarks allow someone who cannot see the screen to learn about its overall makeup. This is the equivalent of how we quickly move our eyes and tilt our heads to different overall areas when scanning the screen to initially learn the overall layout of an experience.

I am hesitant to wrap chat messages in section or other landmark elements. The reason for this is that they “pollute” the list of landmarks a screen reader can generate, making navigation more laborious. This is especially relevant for long-running sessions where many messages are present.

Compare the following and ask yourself which one would be easier to move through with your keyboard if trying to jump from the prompt content area back to the sessions area:.

Here, our visually hidden heading elements serve as a dedicated navigation mechanism for moving through the LLM conversation.

In addition to headings and landmarks, there are two other ways to let people get around rapidly:.

Skip links — sometimes referred to as skip navigation — allow you to quickly jump to another area on the same page or view.

Skip to main content links are commonplace on many mature websites and web apps. Immersive LLM chat experiences should be no different.

Place a skip link in the DOM that allows someone to jump to the main conversation area before any other DOM content that is shown visually on the screen.

Also consider using additional skip links that enable:.

Composite widgets are used when a discrete section of content contains multiple interactive elements. Focus is then managed within this section by the developer, so that:.

According to recent reports, for the purposes of an immersive LLM chat experience, we want to make conversation lists composite widgets. This enables someone to quickly navigate both within and past the entire list.

Here, consider the use case of someone who exclusively relies on a keyboard to navigate. Compare pressing Tab 50 times to get through each of the 50 conversation sessions you’ve created versus pressing Tab once. Now consider motor control conditions where those keypresses can be fatiguing, or even painful to perform.

Once someone places focus on a conversation list composite widget, they can use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through each conversation session list item.

As a quality-of-life improvement, I also like to support the following keyboard interactions:.

To save you a lot of headaches and prototyping: Corner cases around focus management and usability expectations for people who rely exclusively on keyboards work against you if you try to go with a feed pattern approach.

In a recent development, there’s no need to unnecessarily overcomplicate things. The article elements’ wrapping messages with visually-hidden headings approach that I’ve described earlier is both simple and effective.

In a recent development, people who use assistive technology understand the simpler approach, and it involves far less effort to maintain. It’s a win-win!

Industry observers note that pressing F6/Shift+F6 to hop around different areas of the app is an older navigation technique some people who use Windows screen readers employ when navigating through installable desktop apps. Think of it a lot like navigating by landmark.

Recent findings suggest that LLM chat experiences are effectively apps in their own right. Because of this, we can recreate the F6 navigation experience and accommodate those who might attempt it. That means:.

According to recent reports, there’s no secret sauce here. For starters, place an id on each landmark, as well as tabindex="-1". Also ensure each landmark other than main has an accessible name, granted via either aria-label or aria-labelledby.

Recent findings suggest that after that, have an event listener set up to recognize Control+F6 and Control+Shift+F6 key presses. Set focus to:.

Recent findings suggest that and voilà! We now have web-based F6 navigation.

As it is an older technique, people who are younger or less experienced with screen readers may not know F6 navigation exists.

In a recent development, consider socializing the capability in the accessibility portion of your application’s settings menu to address this lack of awareness. Also consider exposing and making F6 navigation re-bindable as another discovery technique, provided your application supports keyboard shortcut rebinding.

Again, this advice only applies to an immersive LLM chat experience. Help agent popups and other less-sophisticated experiences have different expectations.

There are two areas that deserve more finesse when considering where to set focus when F6 navigation is used: the prompting input and the conversation.

Setting focus directly on the input used to type prompts — and not its parent form landmark element — allows someone to rapidly get into the action.

Similarly, setting focus on the visually hidden heading of the last message displayed allows them to quickly jump to the content the LLM generated — a data attribute such as data-last-message can be really helpful for managing this.

Using F6 and Shift+F6 keypresses allows someone to hop from the chat input to what the LLM outputs, then back again. This enables rapid keyboard-based review and iteration on an LLM’s output.

Adjust the text size of your experience and double-check that content is not clipped, or that there’s horizontal overflow.

Industry observers note that people increase the text size of the experiences they use, and more than you’d probably guess. They also resize application windows. Also consider that most LLM-based chat designs tend to use a smaller text size to allow for more information shown on screen.

Because of these two factors, it makes sense to evaluate how your experience holds up when the browser font size is increased.

Customization lives at the heart of accessibility. It’s only natural that LLM-based chat experiences have preferences to better accommodate all the different ways people use them.

In a recent development, in that vein, thoughtful preference offerings can go a long way to helping out people with access needs. Here are some that I’ve found to be particularly useful.

Some LLMs perform interim actions that are circumstantially less vital than the messages they ultimately generate. Here, consider programming-oriented LLMs. They can perform actions like researching and reasoning, code search, and tool calls.

These secondary actions typically have a smaller, less visually vital treatment compared to the messages that contain the main LLM response content. This is because the results are more important than the methodology when using this type of interaction.

Announcing each of these secondary actions could lead to a confusing or overwhelming experience, especially if multiple actions are clustered and fire off live messages in rapid succession.

To address this, you can allow people to circumstantially switch off the announcements for this type of ancillary information. The content in the conversation is still present; it just isn’t unveiled via a live region. This is equivalent to how someone who can see the screen can skim over them.

Sources indicate that letting someone re-enable these types of announcements also grants parity in experience, in that it allows them to know the actions are happening if they want a more information-intensive experience. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, intentionally paying close attention to the LLM’s actions.

Recent findings suggest that it might also be worth investigating letting people toggle visually hiding and showing these less important announcements, as well. This can help people with attention or cognitive considerations, who may be less familiar with technical jargon.

Recent findings suggest that loading animations and large animated effects, like streaming conversations and side panels expanding and collapsing, can be distracting for some people with attention and cognitive considerations. That can go a long way toward breaking someone’s flow.

To address this, you can provide a toggle to turn off animations, reducing their transition time to zero.

It has been revealed that you should also strive to be a respectful and courteous steward of the experience. Default your animation toggle to an off state if a request for a reduced motion experience has been in the device operating system. You can use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to achieve this. Also consider a setting that can re-enable animation, even if a reduced motion request is present.

Some people can get distracted by, or have their focus disrupted by, sound effects. This is similar to animation considerations.

According to recent reports, letting people turn off app-specific sound effects means they don’t have to mute their entire device. Here, consider things like other apps playing flow state-inducing music or white noise that they might be using to help them focus.

Alternatives for sound-based notifications include, but are not limited to:.

I am of the school of thought that any experience that uses keyboard shortcuts also needs to allow both editing and being switched off, both in bulk and on a shortcut-by-shortcut basis.

You may be quick to think of conflicts with assistive technology, but I’d also like to take this space to remind you of different language keyboard layouts.

Live region messages are plain text strings. These strings are announced by screen readers in full in one go from start to end.

In a recent development, semantic information that comes for free by using the appropriate HTML element isn’t present in live region announcements—it’s stripped out. Because of that, we need to think about how we could make our live region content both clear and useful.

Industry observers note that each type of special content has its own considerations. For my work, I created special cases for tables and blocks of code:.

In a recent development, A table’s cell content will sound odd when announced without the companion semantic structure conferred by elements such as table, th, tr, and td. Relationships between columns and rows aren’t present in a live region announcement, either.

Because of this, we can convert the live region announcement of tables to use a concise description of the number of rows and columns, plus a general description and overall trends it might highlight.

A block of code sounds like gibberish when the line breaks are stripped away, and the content is flattened into a single string.

And if it’s a large block of code, it can be a tedious amount of gibberish to parse — nobody wants to sit through an announcement of 2,376 lines of code, painstakingly confirmed character-by-character.

To accommodate this, we can convert the live region announcement of code blocks to use the filename or file type, plus how many lines of code the block contains.

Industry observers note that also note here that people can revisit the actual message content itself. The actual message content will ideally have the appropriate semantics applied to it. This means things like tables being unveiled as, and navigated through as, table content.

In this way, the live region message is a context-setting preview of what to expect. This is the equivalent of promptly visually skimming a message as it is streaming in, then scrolling back to review its content with more attention afterward.

All of the previous is built atop feedback from testing different approaches and noting what works, and what could be improved. You want to facilitate disabled people being the experts in their own lived experience, and not treat others’ advice as the more credible source.

Inclusive user research is a vital way of determining if an experience is actually usable. Centering disabled people’s observations and perspectives is a way to take an experience beyond baseline compliance and create something usable and equitable.

Industry observers note that it is vital to ensure that everyone can use chat-based LLM interactions as the pattern continues to proliferate. Although this is not an exhaustive list of everything you’ll need to do, the content above covers a wide swath of the main places accessibility barriers and friction may show up.

It is my sincerest hope that the improvements I’ve learned about and implemented can help you with your efforts to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who use assistive technology to get what they want or need online.

Thank you to Sarah Higley, whose research and efforts in this area informed key parts of this work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.
  • The old mark was a tree in a circle, and it said too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees.
